title: Write Like You Talk
paragraphs_en: Here's a simple trick for getting more people to read what you write: write in spoken language.

Something comes over most people when they start writing. They write in a different language than they'd use if they were talking to a friend. The sentence structure and even the words are different. No one uses "pen" as a verb in spoken English. You'd feel like an idiot using "pen" instead of "write" in a conversation with a friend.
The last straw for me was a sentence I read a couple days ago:
The mercurial Spaniard himself declared: "After Altamira, all is decadence."
The mercurial Spaniard himself declared: "After Altamira, all is decadence."

It's from Neil Oliver'sA History of Ancient Britain. I feel bad making an example of this book, because it's no worse than lots of others. But just imagine calling Picasso "the mercurial Spaniard" when talking to a friend. Even one sentence of this would raise eyebrows in conversation. And yet people write whole books of it.
Ok, so written and spoken language are different. Does that make written language worse?

If you want people to read and understand what you write, yes. Written language is more complex, which makes it more work to read. It's also more formal and distant, which gives the reader's attention permission to drift. But perhaps worst of all, the complex sentences and fancy words give you, the writer, the false impression that you're saying more than you actually are.

You don't need complex sentences to express complex ideas. When specialists in some abstruse topic talk to one another about ideas in their field, they don't use sentences any more complex than they do when talking about what to have for lunch. They use different words, certainly. But even those they use no more than necessary. And in my experience, the harder the subject, the more informally experts speak. Partly, I think, because they have less to prove, and partly because the harder the ideas you're talking about, the less you can afford to let language get in the way.
Informal language is the athletic clothing of ideas.

I'm not saying spoken language always works best. Poetry is as much music as text, so you can say things you wouldn't say in conversation. And there are a handful of writers who can get away with using fancy language in prose. And then of course there are cases where writers don't want to make it easy to understand what they're saying--in corporate announcements of bad news, for example, or at the morebogusend of the humanities. But for nearly everyone else, spoken language is better.

It seems to be hard for most people to write in spoken language. So perhaps the best solution is to write your first draft the way you usually would, then afterward look at each sentence and ask "Is this the way I'd say this if I were talking to a friend?" If it isn't, imagine what you would say, and use that instead. After a while this filter will start to operate as you write. When you write something you wouldn't say, you'll hear the clank as it hits the page.

Before I publish a new essay, I read it out loud and fix everything that doesn't sound like conversation. I even fix bits that are phonetically awkward; I don't know if that's necessary, but it doesn't cost much.

This trick may not always be enough. I've seen writing so far removed from spoken language that it couldn't be fixed sentence by sentence. For cases like that there's a more drastic solution. After writing the first draft, try explaining to a friend what you just wrote. Then replace the draft with what you said to your friend.

People often tell me how much my essays sound like me talking. The fact that this seems worthy of comment shows how rarely people manage to write in spoken language. Otherwise everyone's writing would sound like them talking.
If you simply manage to write in spoken language, you'll be ahead of 95% of writers. And it's so easy to do: just don't let a sentence through unless it's the way you'd say it to a friend.
Thanksto Patrick Collison and Jessica Livingston for reading drafts of this.
paragraphs_zh: 这里有一个简单的技巧，可以让更多人读你写的东西：用口语来写。
大多数人一开始写东西时，某种东西就会笼罩他们。他们用一种与和朋友交谈时不同的语言来写。句子结构和用词都不同。甚至连他们表达的想法也不同了。他们不会在谈话中说出一些学术垃圾，但当他们写下来时，他们就不再自我检查了。
最后一根稻草是我几天前读到的一句话：
那位多变的西班牙人亲自宣称：'阿尔塔米拉之后，一切都是颓废。'
那位多变的西班牙人亲自宣称：'阿尔塔米拉之后，一切都是颓废。'
这出自 Neil Oliver 的《古代不列颠史》。拿这本书当反面例子让我不好意思，因为它不比其他许多书更差。但试着想象一下把这句话当作对话来说。'那个多变的西班牙人亲自宣称'？你要是在对话中这么说，朋友们会笑你。
好吧，那么书面语和口语是不同的。这是否意味着书面语更差？
如果你希望人们阅读并理解你写的东西，是的。书面语更复杂，这使得阅读更费力。它也更正式，从而与读者产生距离。
你不需要复杂的句子来表达复杂的想法。当某个深奥领域的专家们互相谈论他们领域的想法时，他们不会使用比日常对话更复杂的句子。他们会使用不同的词汇，但即使是这些词汇，他们也不会去挑选那些华丽花哨的。
非正式的语言就是想法的运动服。
我不是说口语总是最好的。诗歌既是音乐也是文字，所以你可以说一些在对话中不会说的话。也有些修辞手法，如果用在对话中会显得做作，但在写作中却很有效，尤其是对于结尾。但对于大多数人来说，大多数时候，像说话一样写作是最好的策略。
对大多数人来说，用口语写作似乎很困难。所以也许最好的解决方案是按你平时的方式写初稿，然后逐句重写，问自己这是不是你在和朋友说话时会说的话。如果不是，想象一下你会怎么说，然后用那种方式来写。
在发表一篇新文章之前，我会把它大声朗读出来，修改一切听起来不像对话的地方。我甚至会修改语音上别扭的地方；我不知道还有谁这样做，但一个句子如果有太多爆破音接近在一起，我会觉得不好。
这个技巧可能并不总是够用。我见过一些写作离口语如此之远，以至于无法逐句修复。对于这种情况，我会建议更剧烈的措施。在你的写作之后，试着用正常的对话来解释你所说的内容。然后用你在对话中说的话代替原来的文字。
人们经常告诉我，我的文章读起来多么像我在说话。这件事看起来值得评论，说明人们多么少能做到用口语写作。如果让你想到的不是'多么不同寻常'，而是'为什么不呢？'，你就走在正确的道路上了。
如果你仅仅做到用口语来写作，你就会领先于95%的写作者。而且这很容易做到：只要不让任何你不会在对话中说的句子通过。用口语来写就行了。
